```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#444444", "#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
old <- options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Custodian", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
f0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
f4 <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * x)
```

Large-sample hydrology studies a method over many catchments at once, so that a pattern is
not mistaken for the quirk of one river. Its weakness is that the truth is never known: a
calibration that scores well may still have the wrong parameters, and nothing in the record
says so.

A large sample of synthetic catchments removes that weakness. Every catchment has its own
climate and its own true model, every truth is written down, and the same automatic
calibration a real study would use is run over all of them. This article does that for 30
catchments and asks three questions:

1. How well does automatic calibration fit, on data it saw and data it did not?
2. Which parameters does it recover, and which does it not?
3. What decides whether a parameter can be recovered?

It then asks what limits automatic calibration, the search or the record, on the same sample,
and finds and scores the floods of a whole batch. [Calibrating many
catchments](many-catchments.html) is the practical runbook for running such a batch.

# The sample

`synthetic_basins()` writes one folder per catchment, in the layout `calibrate_batch()` reads.
Each catchment draws its own climate (how wet, how stormy, how much evaporation) and its own
true parameters, within the calibration bounds. Each record is ten years of daily data,
gauged with persistent error and an extrapolated rating above its highest gauging.

```{r sample}
basins <- file.path(tempdir(), "sample-basins")
output <- file.path(tempdir(), "sample-projects")
unlink(c(basins, output), recursive = TRUE)
sample <- synthetic_basins(basins, n = 30, years = 10, dt = 24, seed = 7)
round(sapply(sample[, c("area_km2", "rain_mm", "pet_mm", "cmax", "kg", "k1", "kb")],
             range), 1)
```

```{r climate, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The sample's climates and catchments. Left: annual rain against potential evaporation. Right: soil capacity against recharge time constant. Each point is one catchment."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.8, 0.8))
plot(sample$pet_mm, sample$rain_mm, pch = 16, col = pal[2], xlab = "PET (mm a year)",
     ylab = "Rain (mm a year)")
plot(sample$cmax, sample$kg, log = "y", pch = 16, col = pal[3], xlab = "cmax (mm)",
     ylab = "kg (hours, log scale)")
```

The sample spans rain from `r f0(min(sample$rain_mm))` to `r f0(max(sample$rain_mm))` mm a
year, areas from `r f0(min(sample$area_km2))` to `r f0(max(sample$area_km2))` km2, and soil
capacities from `r f0(min(sample$cmax))` to `r f0(max(sample$cmax))` mm. Climate and
catchment are drawn independently, as they would not be in nature, so that their effects
can be told apart.

# Calibrating all of them

One call calibrates the whole sample: automatic calibration of all seven parameters at once
from the standard preset, with four starts, in parallel workers. Each record's two wettest
years are held back and revealed at the end by the test, as every project does by default.

```{r batch}
# R CMD check allows two processes; elsewhere use up to four cores. The results do not depend
# on the number: each basin's random starts are seeded from its name.
limited <- identical(toupper(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_")), "TRUE")
cores <- if (limited) 2L else min(4L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
# Each basin's rain is biased by a known factor between 0.9 and 1.1, so the rainfall factor,
# locked by default, is searched.
unlock <- list(fc = c(0.6, 1.6))
elapsed <- system.time(
  calibrate_batch(basins, output, starts = 4, control = list(maxit = 40), cores = cores,
                  overrides = unlock, test = TRUE)
)[["elapsed"]]
status <- batch_status(output)
table(status$state)
results <- batch_results(output)
```

```{r batch-numbers, include=FALSE}
minutes <- elapsed / 60
```

All `r sum(status$state == "done")` catchments finished, in `r f0(minutes)` minutes on
`r cores` cores. A sample of hundreds takes the same call; `calibrate_batch()` resumes where
it stopped if interrupted. [Calibrating many catchments](many-catchments.html) covers
running it for real.

# How well does it fit?

```{r scores, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The share of catchments reaching each score, on the calibration window, the validation window and the held-back wettest years."}
scores <- list(calibration = results$candidate_score, validation = results$validation_score,
               `wettest years` = results$wettest_score)
plot(NA, xlim = range(unlist(scores), na.rm = TRUE), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "NSE",
     ylab = "Share of catchments at or below")
for (i in seq_along(scores)) {
  lines(stats::ecdf(scores[[i]]), col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2, do.points = FALSE)
}
legend("topleft", names(scores), col = pal[2:4], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
round(sapply(scores, stats::quantile, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), na.rm = TRUE), 3)
```

```{r score-numbers, include=FALSE}
med <- vapply(scores, stats::median, 0, na.rm = TRUE)
worst <- results$project[which.min(results$validation_score)]
```

The median catchment scores `r f3(med[["calibration"]])` on calibration,
`r f3(med[["validation"]])` on validation and `r f3(med[["wettest years"]])` on the held-back
wettest years. By the usual standard every one of these is an excellent fit. The weakest on
validation is `r worst`, at `r f3(min(results$validation_score))`. If scores were the whole
story, this would be the end of the article.

# Which parameters does it recover?

Every calibrated value can be set against its truth. The two surface stores of a cascade can
swap without changing the flow, so they are compared as the faster and the slower of the
pair.

```{r recovery}
fitted_config <- function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  read_entry(project, read_projects(project)$candidate)$configuration
}
values <- function(cfg) {
  k <- sort(c(cfg$surface$k1, cfg$surface$k2))
  c(fc = cfg$fc, cmax = cfg$distribution$cmax, b = cfg$distribution$b,
    kg = cfg$recharge$kg, k_fast = k[1], k_slow = k[2], kb = cfg$groundwater$kb)
}
truth <- t(vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  values(read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml")))
}, numeric(7)))
fitted <- t(vapply(sample$basin, function(id) values(fitted_config(id)), numeric(7)))
# The typical error is the median, across catchments, of the size of the error as a factor:
# 0.1 means the fitted value is typically about 10 per cent off, either way.
typical <- apply(abs(log(fitted / truth)), 2, stats::median)
data.frame(parameter = names(typical), typical_error = round(exp(typical) - 1, 3),
           within_10_percent = colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1)),
           row.names = NULL)
```

```{r recovery-plot, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Calibrated against true values, one point per catchment. Points on the line are exact. Log scales for the parameters that span orders of magnitude."}
logged <- c("kg", "k_fast", "k_slow", "kb")
par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 1.6, 0.6), cex.main = 1)
for (p in colnames(truth)) {
  lim <- range(c(truth[, p], fitted[, p]))
  plot(truth[, p], fitted[, p], log = if (p %in% logged) "xy" else "", xlim = lim, ylim = lim,
       pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.7), xlab = "true", ylab = "calibrated", main = p)
  abline(0, 1, col = pal[7], lty = 2, untf = TRUE)
}
```

```{r ranking, include=FALSE}
order_by <- names(sort(typical))
pct <- function(p) f0(100 * (exp(typical[[p]]) - 1))
best_two <- min(colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1))[order_by[1:2]])
best_two_text <- if (best_two == nrow(truth)) {
  paste("all", nrow(truth), "catchments")
} else {
  paste(best_two, "or more of the", nrow(truth), "catchments")
}
```

```{r edges, include=FALSE}
# A calibrated value within 1 per cent of a bound (in logs for log-scaled parameters) means the
# search ended against the fence rather than at an optimum inside it.
b <- calibration_bounds(pdm_presets("standard"), overrides = unlock)
at_edge <- vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  cfg <- fitted_config(id)
  v <- vapply(b$path, function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(cfg, p), numeric(1))
  lo <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(b$lower), b$lower)
  hi <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(b$upper), b$upper)
  x <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(v), v)
  any(x - lo < 0.01 * (hi - lo) | hi - x < 0.01 * (hi - lo))
}, logical(1))
edge_ids <- names(at_edge)[at_edge]
```

`r if (length(edge_ids)) paste0(length(edge_ids), " calibration", if (length(edge_ids) > 1) "s" else "", " (", paste(edge_ids, collapse = ", "), ") ended with a parameter against a bound. That is worth checking in a real study: it can mean a search that went astray, or a true value close to the bound. Nothing in the batch flags it yet, so check for it as this article does.") else "No calibration ended with a parameter against a bound."`

The ranking is clear. `r order_by[1]` and `r order_by[2]` come back closest, typically within
`r pct(order_by[1])` and `r pct(order_by[2])` per cent. `r order_by[7]` and `r order_by[6]`
are the worst, typically `r pct(order_by[7])` and `r pct(order_by[6])` per cent out. Yet the
calibrations that got them wrong still score an excellent NSE. A good score shows that the
model reproduces the record; it does not show that the parameters are right.

# Did the search find the best fit?

A parameter that comes back wrong has two possible causes. The search may have stopped short
of the best fit, or the record may not be able to tell the true value from the wrong one.
The truth settles which: score each catchment's true parameters on the same calibration
window, and set the calibration's score against it.

```{r against-truth}
true_score <- vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  entries <- read_project(project)$entries
  fit <- utils::tail(entries$id[entries$type == "auto_calibration"], 1)
  cfg <- read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml"))
  changes <- vapply(b$path, function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(cfg, p), numeric(1))
  suppressWarnings(preview_trial(project, fit, changes))$scores$nse
}, numeric(1))
calibrated_score <- results$candidate_score[match(sample$basin, results$project)]
gap <- calibrated_score - true_score
round(c(at_least_truth = sum(gap >= -1e-6), short_by_over_0.001 = sum(gap < -0.001),
        largest_shortfall = max(0, -min(gap))), 4)
```

```{r truth-numbers, include=FALSE}
n_match <- sum(gap >= -1e-6)
n_short <- sum(gap < -0.001)
```

In `r n_match` of the `r length(gap)` catchments the calibration scores at least as well as
the true parameters`r if (n_short == 0) paste0(if (n_match < length(gap)) paste0(", and in the other", if (length(gap) - n_match > 1) "s" else "", " it falls short by no more than ", sprintf("%.4f", max(0, -min(gap))), " in NSE") else "") else paste0("; in ", n_short, " it falls short by more than 0.001")`.
`r if (n_short == 0) paste0("The search found the best fit each record allows. So when ", order_by[7], " comes back ", pct(order_by[7]), " per cent out, the search is not to blame: parameter sets that far apart fit the record equally well, and the record, with its gauge error, cannot choose between them. More model runs, or a different search, would not recover it.") else "Those catchments are search failures, and their parameters say nothing about what the record can recover."`

Why can the record not see `kb`? Water reaches the groundwater store as recharge, which is
already slow; a groundwater store faster than its recharge passes it on almost unchanged, so
across a hundredfold range of `kb` the flow hardly changes. The parameter matters only when
recharge stops, in a drought long enough to empty the soil, and there equally good
calibrations can disagree widely.
[What limits automatic calibration](large-sample.html#what-limits-automatic-calibration) shows this with profiles and
drought scenarios, and compares four searches on this sample.

# What decides whether a parameter can be recovered?

A parameter can be recovered only if the record exercises it. A natural guess is that the soil
capacity is pinned best where the climate works the soil hardest: in a dry climate the soil
fills and empties far enough for its size to show, while in a wet one many capacities fit the
record equally well. A simple measure of how hard the climate works the soil is its dryness,
potential evaporation over rain. The sample can test the guess.

```{r dryness, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The error in each catchment's calibrated soil capacity against the dryness of its climate."}
dryness <- sample$pet_mm / sample$rain_mm
cmax_error <- abs(log(fitted[, "cmax"] / truth[, "cmax"]))
plot(dryness, cmax_error, pch = 16, col = pal[3], xlab = "Dryness (PET / rain)",
     ylab = "cmax error (|log ratio|)")
rho <- stats::cor(dryness, cmax_error, method = "spearman")
round(rho, 2)
```

```{r rho-numbers, include=FALSE}
direction <- if (rho < -0.3) "drier" else if (rho > 0.3) "wetter" else NULL
```

`r if (!is.null(direction)) paste0("Across the sample, the soil capacity is recovered better in ", direction, " climates (Spearman correlation ", f2(rho), " between dryness and the size of the error).") else paste0("Across this sample, dryness alone does not explain how well the soil capacity is recovered (Spearman correlation ", f2(rho), "): other things, such as how the parameters trade off against each other, matter as much.")`
A real large-sample study can ask the same question of its own results, but cannot see the
error itself; here it can.

# The largest floods

The test also revealed each record's two wettest years. Their peaks are above the highest
gauging, where the rating records them low, so the recorded peak is not the truth. Here the
true peak is known.

```{r peaks}
peak_rows <- lapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  entries <- read_project(project)$entries
  test <- read_entry(project, utils::tail(entries$id[entries$type == "test"], 1))
  forcing <- data.table::fread(file.path(basins, id, "forcing.csv"))
  forcing$time <- as.POSIXct(forcing$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
  true_flow <- synthetic_catchment(forcing, read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml")),
                                   error = list(sd = 0, memory_h = 72))$true_flow
  reg <- read_entry(project, entries$id[entries$type == "data_registered"][1])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(test$wettest$years), function(i) {
    y <- test$wettest$years[[i]]
    span <- reg$scorecard$wettest$years[[i]]
    data.frame(basin = id, recorded = y$observed_peak_m3s, calibrated = y$simulated_peak_m3s,
               true = max(true_flow[span$first_row:span$last_row]),
               low = y$spread_low_m3s, high = y$spread_high_m3s)
  }))
})
peaks <- do.call(rbind, peak_rows)
vs_recorded <- peaks$calibrated / peaks$recorded - 1
vs_true <- peaks$calibrated / peaks$true - 1
round(c(median_error_vs_recorded = stats::median(vs_recorded),
        median_error_vs_true = stats::median(vs_true),
        median_spread = stats::median((peaks$high - peaks$low) / peaks$true),
        share_true_inside_spread = mean(peaks$true >= peaks$low & peaks$true <= peaks$high)), 3)
```

```{r peak-plot, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Peak error in the held-back wettest years, judged against the recorded peak (which the rating understates) and against the true peak."}
boxplot(list(`against recorded peak` = 100 * vs_recorded, `against true peak` = 100 * vs_true),
        horizontal = TRUE, col = adjustcolor(pal[2:3], 0.4), xlab = "Peak error (per cent)",
        las = 1, cex.axis = 0.85)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = pal[7])
```

```{r peak-numbers, include=FALSE}
inside <- mean(peaks$true >= peaks$low & peaks$true <= peaks$high)
```

Judged against the recorded peaks, the calibrated models look
`r f0(abs(100 * stats::median(vs_recorded)))` per cent
`r if (stats::median(vs_recorded) > 0) "high" else "low"` in the median year. Judged against
the true peaks, they are `r f0(abs(100 * stats::median(vs_true)))` per cent
`r if (stats::median(vs_true) > 0) "high" else "low"`. Across the
`r nrow(peaks)` held-back years, the range of the equally good fits contains the true peak in
`r f0(100 * inside)` per cent of them. [Larger floods](extrapolation.html) explains these
checks for one catchment; across a sample, they show how far a method can be trusted with
floods it has not seen.

# What the sample shows

- **Scores are not evidence of correct parameters.** Every catchment scored an NSE of at
  least `r f2(min(results$validation_score))` on validation. Some parameters were still
  recovered poorly, and only the known truth shows it.
- **The search is not the limit.** In `r n_match` of `r length(gap)` catchments the
  calibration fitted at least as well as the truth. What the record cannot recover, no search
  will.
- **Some parameters are reliably recovered and some are not.** Here `r order_by[1]` and
  `r order_by[2]` were within 10 per cent in `r best_two_text`; `r order_by[7]` was within 10 per cent in
  only `r colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1))[[order_by[7]]]` of them. A study that
  reads meaning into a parameter should first know which kind it is.
- **A rating extrapolated above the highest gauging makes a good model look bad on the
  biggest floods.** Judge peak errors with the rating flag in mind.
- **Simple explanations need testing.** The guess that dry climates pin the soil store better
  was `r if (identical(direction, "drier")) "borne out" else "not borne out"` here; a large sample is
  where such guesses are tested.
- **Large samples answer questions single catchments cannot**: which parameters to trust,
  under which climates, and how much a calibration method can be relied on beyond its record.

For a real study, replace `synthetic_basins()` with real basin folders and keep everything
else. Running a synthetic sample alongside, made to resemble the real catchments with
`fit_rain()` and sensible ranges, shows how far the method can be trusted before the real
results are read.

# What limits automatic calibration


When a calibrated parameter comes back wrong, either the search stopped short of the best
fit or the record cannot tell the right value from the wrong one. The two call for opposite
remedies: a better search in the first case, and in the second, more information or a fixed
value. On real data they cannot be told apart, because the best possible fit is unknown.

On synthetic catchments they can. Each catchment's true parameters are known, so they can be
scored on the same record as the calibration. A calibration that scores at least as well as
the truth has found the best fit the record allows, and any parameter it still gets wrong is
beyond the record's reach. This article applies that test to the sample of 30 catchments in
[A large sample](large-sample.html) and follows where it leads: to a fault in staged
calibration, now fixed; to one parameter, `kb`, that no search can recover; and to the one
kind of event in which that parameter matters.

## The question

[A large sample](large-sample.html) found most parameters recovered closely and one, `kb`,
the groundwater store's constant, recovered poorly. The obvious suspect was the search.
`calibrate_pdm()` uses L-BFGS-B, which follows the slope of the objective, estimated by
nudging each parameter in turn. A model with thresholds and stores that switch on and off can
have a rough objective that misleads such a search, and hydrology has long preferred global
methods for that reason. One of them, dynamically dimensioned search (DDS; Tolson and
Shoemaker, 2007), is built for watershed models and now available as `method = "dds"`.

## Four searches, one sample

Each search was run as one `calibrate_batch()` over the same 30 catchments, ten years of daily
data each, and every result was set against its truth. Each catchment's rain is biased by a
known factor, so every search included the rainfall factor `fc`, which a batch now holds at 1
unless an override unlocks it.

| Search | What it does |
|---|---|
| staged, confined polish | Water balance and slow stores, then fast stores, then a polish of everything kept within a quarter of each range around stage 2's values (before version 0.8.0) |
| staged | The same, with the polish free to search the full bounds (now the default) |
| all at once | All seven parameters in one search, from four starts |
| staged, DDS | The staged search with DDS, given the same number of model runs as the first |

The four batches take too long to repeat when this page is built, so their results are
stored with the package. The minutes are for four cores, except the confined polish, which
the benchmark has to run on one. `inst/benchmarks/search_methods.R` reruns them; each basin's
searches are seeded, so a rerun gives the same numbers.

```{r study}
study <- utils::read.csv(system.file("extdata", "search_study.csv", package = "pdmS7"))
searches <- c("staged, confined polish", "staged", "all at once", "staged, DDS")
gap <- study$nse - study$true_nse
summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(searches, function(s) {
  k <- study$search == s
  data.frame(search = s, model_runs = stats::median(study$model_runs[k]),
             minutes = study$batch_minutes[k][1], at_least_truth = sum(gap[k] >= -1e-6),
             short_by_over_0.001 = sum(gap[k] < -0.001), largest_shortfall = max(0, -min(gap[k])))
}))
summary_table$largest_shortfall <- round(summary_table$largest_shortfall, 4)
summary_table
```

```{r study-numbers, include=FALSE}
row <- function(s) summary_table[summary_table$search == s, ]
failed <- study$basin[study$search == "staged, confined polish" & gap < -0.001]
dds_short <- row("staged, DDS")$short_by_over_0.001
```

The search was not the problem. Calibrating everything at once with L-BFGS-B scored at least
as well as the truth in `r row("all at once")$at_least_truth` of 30 catchments and was never
short by more than `r f4(row("all at once")$largest_shortfall)` in NSE, in
`r f1(row("all at once")$minutes)` minutes on four cores. DDS, with the same budget as the
staged search, fell short by more than 0.001 in `r dds_short` catchments. DDS is designed for
budgets of thousands of runs per search; here it had about
`r f0(row("staged, DDS")$model_runs / 6)` for each of its six searches per catchment, and on a smooth objective such as NSE the slope-following search makes better use
of them.

## Where the staged search went wrong

The confined polish failed twice, in `r paste(failed, collapse = " and ")`.

```{r trap}
# The same 30 catchments as above.
sample_path <- basins
trapped <- study[study$search == "staged, confined polish" & study$basin %in% failed,
                 c("basin", "nse", "true_nse")]
cbind(trapped, sample[match(trapped$basin, sample$basin), c("k1", "k2")])
```

```{r trap-numbers, include=FALSE}
slow <- range(unlist(sample[match(failed, sample$basin), c("k1", "k2")]))
median_k1 <- stats::median(sample$k1)
```

Both have slow surface stores, between `r f0(slow[1])` and `r f0(slow[2])` hours against a
sample median of `r f0(median_k1)` for the first store. Stage 1 fits the water balance and the
slow stores with the surface stores held at their starting values, 2 and 4 hours. Where the
true surface stores are much slower, stage 1 can make up for them with the wrong slow stores,
and a polish kept near that point cannot leave it. Whether it happens depends on where stage 1
lands, which is why it struck `r length(failed)` catchments in 30 and not every one with slow
surface stores. With the polish over the full bounds, the staged search fell short of the
truth by more than 0.001 in `r if (row("staged")$short_by_over_0.001 == 0) "none of them" else paste(row("staged")$short_by_over_0.001, "of them")`.
Since version 0.8.0 that is the default.

## What the record cannot tell: kb

With the search cleared, the parameters it gets wrong tell what the record cannot. Here is
each search's typical error by parameter: the median, across catchments, of how far the
calibrated value is from the truth, as a fraction. The surface stores are compared as the
faster and slower of the pair, since they can swap without changing the flow.

```{r study-recovery}
truth <- sample[, c("basin", "fc", "cmax", "b", "kg", "k1", "k2", "kb")]
ordered <- function(d) {
  k <- cbind(d$k1, d$k2)
  d$k_fast <- pmin(k[, 1], k[, 2])
  d$k_slow <- pmax(k[, 1], k[, 2])
  d
}
truth <- ordered(truth)
params <- c("fc", "cmax", "b", "kg", "k_fast", "k_slow", "kb")
recovery <- t(vapply(searches, function(s) {
  fit <- ordered(study[study$search == s, ])
  tr <- truth[match(fit$basin, truth$basin), ]
  vapply(params, function(p) exp(stats::median(abs(log(fit[[p]] / tr[[p]])))) - 1, numeric(1))
}, numeric(length(params))))
round(recovery, 2)
```

`r if (all(colnames(recovery)[apply(recovery, 1, which.max)] == "kb")) "Every search, good or bad, leaves \x60kb\x60 the worst recovered." else "\x60kb\x60 is among the worst recovered under every search."` A search that reaches the truth's
score and still misses a parameter by that much is meeting a flat objective. The direct test
is a profile: fix `kb` at a range of values, recalibrate everything else at each one, and
record the best score. If the profile is flat, the record does not constrain `kb`. Holding the
other parameters at their true values as well shows how much of the flatness is `kb` barely
mattering, and how much is the others making up for it.

```{r profile}
others <- c("fc", "distribution.cmax", "distribution.b", "recharge.kg", "surface.k1",
            "surface.k2")
kb_grid <- 10^seq(2, 6, by = 0.5)
basin_data <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path(sample_path, id)
  forcing <- as.data.frame(data.table::fread(file.path(dir, "forcing.csv")))
  forcing$time <- as.POSIXct(forcing$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
  meta <- yaml::read_yaml(file.path(dir, "basin.yml"))
  day <- format(forcing$time, "%Y-%m-%d")
  list(forcing = forcing, observed = data.table::fread(file.path(dir, "flow.csv"))$q_m3s,
       truth = read_pdm_config(file.path(dir, "truth.yml")),
       first = match(meta$calibration[[1]], day), last = match(meta$calibration[[2]], day))
}
simulate <- function(cfg, forcing, start_flow) {
  model <- pdm_from_config(cfg)
  state <- suppressWarnings(initial_state_from_flow(model, start_flow, baseflow_fraction = 0.7))
  run_pdm(model, forcing[c("rain", "pet")], state)$output$q_m3s
}
nse_on <- function(sim, obs) 1 - sum((sim - obs)^2) / sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)
profile_basin <- function(id) {
  d <- basin_data(id)
  rows <- d$first:d$last
  cal <- d$forcing[seq_len(d$last), ]
  obs <- d$observed[seq_len(d$last)]
  b <- calibration_bounds(d$truth, overrides = list(fc = c(0.6, 1.6)))
  b <- b[b$path %in% others, ]
  fits <- lapply(kb_grid, function(kb) {
    cfg <- d$truth
    cfg$groundwater$kb <- kb
    held <- nse_on(simulate(cfg, cal, obs[1])[rows], obs[rows])
    fit <- suppressWarnings(calibrate_pdm(
      cfg, cal[c("rain", "pet")], obs, stats::setNames(b$lower, b$path),
      stats::setNames(b$upper, b$path), warmup = d$first - 1, objective = "nse",
      control = list(maxit = 60), starts = 2, seed = 1, log_scale = b$path[b$scale == "log"]
    ))
    list(held = held, refit = 1 - fit$objective, config = fit$config)
  })
  list(id = id, data = d, fits = fits,
       table = data.frame(basin = id, kb = kb_grid,
                          others_at_truth = vapply(fits, function(f) f$held, numeric(1)),
                          others_recalibrated = vapply(fits, function(f) f$refit, numeric(1))))
}
profiles <- lapply(c("S001", "S002", "S003"), profile_basin)
```

```{r profile-plot, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Best calibration NSE with kb fixed, one panel per catchment, each axis spanning the same range of NSE. Grey: every other parameter at its true value. Blue: every other parameter recalibrated. The dashed line marks the true kb."}
# The same span of NSE in every panel, so that a flat profile looks flat everywhere.
span <- max(vapply(profiles, function(p) {
  diff(range(c(p$table$others_at_truth, p$table$others_recalibrated)))
}, numeric(1)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4.2, 1.6, 0.6), cex.main = 1)
for (p in profiles) {
  t <- p$table
  top <- max(c(t$others_at_truth, t$others_recalibrated))
  plot(t$kb, t$others_recalibrated, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 16, col = pal[2],
       ylim = c(top - span, top), xlab = "kb (fixed)", ylab = "NSE", main = p$id)
  lines(t$kb, t$others_at_truth, type = "b", pch = 1, col = pal[7])
  abline(v = p$data$truth$groundwater$kb, lty = 2, col = pal[3])
}
```

```{r profile-numbers}
mid <- kb_grid >= 100 & kb_grid <= 1e4
flatness <- do.call(rbind, lapply(profiles, function(p) {
  t <- p$table
  data.frame(basin = p$id, true_kb = p$data$truth$groundwater$kb,
             range_others_at_truth = diff(range(t$others_at_truth[mid])),
             range_others_recalibrated = diff(range(t$others_recalibrated[mid])),
             drop_at_1e6 = max(t$others_recalibrated) - t$others_recalibrated[length(kb_grid)])
}))
flatness[-1] <- round(flatness[-1], 4)
flatness
```

```{r flat-numbers, include=FALSE}
held_max <- max(flatness$range_others_at_truth)
refit_max <- max(flatness$range_others_recalibrated)
```

Across a hundredfold range of `kb`, from 100 to 10,000, the best NSE moves by no more than
`r f4(refit_max)` with the other parameters recalibrated, and by no more than
`r f4(held_max)` with them held at the truth. The second number is the telling one: even with
nothing making up for it, changing `kb` a hundredfold barely changes the flow. The record
does not constrain `kb` because, over that range, `kb` hardly affects the flow. Only very slow
values cost more: at 1,000,000 the best NSE drops by up to `r f3(max(flatness$drop_at_1e6))`. This is equifinality in its plainest
form: many values of a parameter fit the record equally well.

The reason lies in how water reaches the groundwater store. It arrives as recharge, which
drains from the soil with time constant `kg`, typically thousands of hours in this sample.
That recharge is already slow and smooth. A groundwater store that responds faster than it
passes the recharge on almost unchanged, so the flow shows the slower of the two stores in
series, `kg`, and hides the faster, `kb`. That is why `kg` is recovered within a few per cent
and `kb` is not.

## Where kb matters: drought

A parameter the record cannot see may still matter for events the record does not contain.
`kb` sets how fast the groundwater store drains on its own, which it does only when recharge
stops, and recharge stops only when the soil is dry. So the equally good fits from the
profiles, with `kb` at about 300, 3,000 and 30,000, are run through two droughts, each
starting on 1 April 2018 in the validation period:

- **A dry summer:** six months at 30 per cent of the recorded rain.
- **A long drought:** twelve months with no rain at all.

```{r drought}
# The fits with kb at about 300, 3,000 and 30,000.
kb_sets <- vapply(c(2.5, 3.5, 4.5), function(x) which.min(abs(log10(kb_grid) - x)), integer(1))
scenario <- function(forcing, months, share) {
  out <- forcing
  begin <- as.POSIXct("2018-04-01", tz = "UTC")
  end <- seq(begin, by = paste(months, "months"), length.out = 2)[2]
  window <- out$time >= begin & out$time < end
  out$rain[window] <- share * out$rain[window]
  list(forcing = out, window = window)
}
drought <- do.call(rbind, lapply(profiles, function(p) {
  d <- p$data
  cases <- list(`dry summer` = scenario(d$forcing, 6, 0.3),
                `long drought` = scenario(d$forcing, 12, 0))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cases), function(name) {
    s <- cases[[name]]
    true_low <- min(simulate(d$truth, s$forcing, d$observed[1])[s$window])
    usual_low <- min(simulate(d$truth, d$forcing, d$observed[1])[s$window])
    ratios <- vapply(kb_sets, function(i) {
      min(simulate(p$fits[[i]]$config, s$forcing, d$observed[1])[s$window]) / true_low
    }, numeric(1))
    usual <- vapply(kb_sets, function(i) {
      min(simulate(p$fits[[i]]$config, d$forcing, d$observed[1])[s$window]) / usual_low
    }, numeric(1))
    soil <- {
      model <- pdm_from_config(d$truth)
      state <- suppressWarnings(initial_state_from_flow(model, d$observed[1],
                                                        baseflow_fraction = 0.7))
      run_pdm(model, s$forcing[c("rain", "pet")], state)$output$soil_mm
    }
    fit_scores <- vapply(kb_sets, function(i) p$fits[[i]]$refit, numeric(1))
    data.frame(
      basin = p$id, scenario = name, true_soil_at_end_mm = soil[max(which(s$window))],
      nse_spread = diff(range(fit_scores)),
      low_flow_vs_truth_min = min(ratios), low_flow_vs_truth_max = max(ratios),
      same_window_no_drought_min = min(usual), same_window_no_drought_max = max(usual)
    )
  }))
}))
drought[-(1:2)] <- round(drought[-(1:2)], 3)
drought
```

```{r drought-numbers, include=FALSE}
summer <- drought[drought$scenario == "dry summer", ]
long <- drought[drought$scenario == "long drought", ]
summer_band <- range(c(summer$low_flow_vs_truth_min, summer$low_flow_vs_truth_max))
long_band <- range(c(long$low_flow_vs_truth_min, long$low_flow_vs_truth_max))
long_factor <- max(long$low_flow_vs_truth_max / long$low_flow_vs_truth_min)
usual_band <- range(c(drought$same_window_no_drought_min, drought$same_window_no_drought_max))
```

The three parameter sets of each catchment fit the record to within
`r f4(max(drought$nse_spread))` in NSE. Without any drought, their lowest flows in the same
months lie between `r f2(usual_band[1])` and `r f2(usual_band[2])` times the truth's. Through
the dry summer, the soil keeps water, recharge continues, and the band is much the same:
`r f2(summer_band[1])` to `r f2(summer_band[2])`, with at least
`r f0(min(summer$true_soil_at_end_mm))` mm still in the true soil store at the end. Through
the long drought, the soil empties (to `r f1(max(long$true_soil_at_end_mm))` mm or less),
recharge stops, the groundwater store drains at the rate `kb` sets, and the band opens to
`r f2(long_band[1])` to `r f2(long_band[2])` times the true lowest flow.

So `kb` is harmless within the record and decisive beyond it. Equally good calibrations agree
on the floods and droughts they were fitted to, and can disagree by a factor of up to
`r f1(long_factor)` in the lowest flow of a drought severe enough to stop recharge. It is the low-flow counterpart of the extrapolated
rating at the top end ([Larger floods](extrapolation.html)): a model can be trusted only as
far as its record exercised it.

## Which groundwater store?

`kb` cannot be identified within one store. A related question is whether the record can
choose the store itself: linear, quadratic, cubic or exponential. [Recession
analysis](../reference/recession_analysis.html) suggests it might, from data alone. Once the
surface stores have drained, the rate at which flow falls against the flow itself, on log
axes, has a slope of 1, 1.5, 1.67 or 2 for the four stores.

The test used sixteen made-up catchments: each store, under standard recharge (the soil store
drains to groundwater all the time) and split recharge (groundwater fills only when runoff
does), on two ten-year hourly rain records with 3% gauge noise. Each catchment was calibrated
with all four stores on seven years and scored on the last three. Four ways of choosing were
compared: the slope read straight off the record, the best validation NSE, the best
validation log NSE, and the fitted store whose simulated recession slope comes closest to the
record's. The script is `inst/benchmarks/recession_stores.R`.

```{r stores}
stores <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "recession_stores.csv", package = "pdmS7"))
theory <- c(linear = 1, quadratic = 1.5, cubic = 5 / 3, exponential = 2)
cases <- split(stores, list(stores$truth, stores$recharge, stores$seed), drop = TRUE)
chosen <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cases, function(x) {
  ranked <- order(-x$val_log_nse)
  data.frame(
    recharge = x$recharge[1], truth = x$truth[1],
    slope_read = names(theory)[which.min(abs(theory - x$observed_slope[1]))],
    best_nse = x$candidate[which.max(x$val_nse)],
    best_log_nse = x$candidate[ranked[1]],
    closest_simulated_slope = x$candidate[which.min(abs(x$simulated_slope -
                                                          x$observed_slope))],
    log_nse_margin = x$val_log_nse[ranked[1]] - x$val_log_nse[ranked[2]]
  )
}))
right <- function(rule) tapply(chosen[[rule]] == chosen$truth, chosen$recharge, sum)
rules <- c("slope_read", "best_nse", "best_log_nse", "closest_simulated_slope")
correct <- t(vapply(rules, right, c(split = 0, standard = 0)))
cbind(correct, all = rowSums(correct))
margins <- chosen$log_nse_margin
```

```{r stores-numbers, include=FALSE}
n_case <- nrow(chosen)
within_tie <- sum(margins < 0.02)
```

The validation scores found the true store in every catchment. Neither recession rule did as
well:

- **The slope read off the record** worked under split recharge but not standard. Recharge
  that continues through a recession slows its fall, and the slopes came out 0.1 to 0.9 low,
  so nearly every store looked linear. Even with split recharge, the exponential store's slope
  (about 1.8) sat nearer the cubic's 1.67 than its own 2.
- **Matching the simulated recession slope** did little better. Each fitted store bends its
  parameters until its recessions look roughly right, so the slopes no longer separate them.

The validation scores won, but only just. The best store's log NSE beat the next by a median
of `r f4(stats::median(margins))`, at most `r f3(max(margins))`, and in
`r within_tie` of `r n_case` catchments by less than 0.02, the tolerance within which a
calibration project counts two scores as equally good. These records came from the model
being fitted, with small, simple noise. Real records add rain errors and a structure that is
never exactly right, and margins of a few thousandths would not survive them.

So the record can choose the groundwater store only in principle. In practice, compare the
stores, report the ones within the tolerance of the best as equally good, and keep the
standard cubic store unless one is clearly better. Use the recession plot as a check that a
fitted model's low flows fall at the right rate, not as a way to choose its store.

## Which recharge rule?

The same test for recharge used nine made-up catchments: standard recharge (the soil store
drains to groundwater all the time), split recharge (a share of each event's runoff goes to
groundwater) and demand recharge (groundwater draws fastest when it is emptiest), each on
three ten-year hourly rain records with the cubic store and 3% gauge noise. Each was
calibrated with all three rules. The script is `inst/benchmarks/recharge_rules.R`.

```{r recharge}
rules <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "recharge_rules.csv", package = "pdmS7"))
cases <- split(rules, list(rules$truth, rules$seed), drop = TRUE)
picked <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cases, function(x) {
  by_log <- order(-x$val_log_nse)
  by_nse <- order(-x$val_nse)
  data.frame(truth = x$truth[1], best_log_nse = x$candidate[by_log[1]],
             log_nse_margin = x$val_log_nse[by_log[1]] - x$val_log_nse[by_log[2]],
             best_nse = x$candidate[by_nse[1]],
             nse_margin = x$val_nse[by_nse[1]] - x$val_nse[by_nse[2]],
             rise_follows_quick_flow = x$observed_rise_cor[1])
}))
rownames(picked) <- NULL
picked[order(picked$truth), ]
```

```{r recharge-numbers, include=FALSE}
log_margins <- picked$log_nse_margin
split_rise <- picked$rise_follows_quick_flow[picked$truth == "split"]
other_rise <- picked$rise_follows_quick_flow[picked$truth != "split"]
```

Here the record speaks clearly. The validation scores picked the true rule in all
`r nrow(picked)` catchments, and by margins in log NSE of `r f2(min(log_margins))` to
`r f2(max(log_margins))`, against a median of `r f4(stats::median(margins))` for the
groundwater store. A wrong recharge rule cannot be hidden by the other parameters: it changes
when groundwater fills, and so the shape of every recession and the level of every low flow.
Margins this size should survive the errors of real data, though only a test on gauged
catchments can show it.

One diagnostic needs no model. Across each event, the rise of the baseflow line that
[`find_events()`](../reference/find_events.html) draws can be set against the event's quick
flow. Split recharge feeds groundwater in proportion to each event's runoff, so the two move
together: their correlation was `r f2(min(split_rise))` to `r f2(max(split_rise))` under split
recharge, and `r f2(min(other_rise))` to `r f2(max(other_rise))` under the other two. It
separates split recharge from the rest, but not standard from demand.

## What the study shows

- **Check the search against the truth before blaming it.** Scoring the true parameters
  separates a weak search from a weak record. Here the search was sound.
- **Calibrate all at once, or in stages with a free polish.** Both reach the best fit the
  record allows. A polish confined near stage 2 can lock in a wrong first stage; it is no
  longer the default.
- **Use DDS for rough objectives, not smooth ones.** At equal budget it lost to L-BFGS-B on
  NSE. It suits threshold objectives and large budgets.
- **Do not report `kb` as calibrated.** The record cannot identify it. Fix it from regional
  knowledge and leave it out of the search (`exclude = "groundwater.kb"` in
  `calibrate_batch()` and `pdm_stages()`), or calibrate it and report the range of equally
  good values instead of one number.
- **Do not expect the record to choose the groundwater store.** Validation scores picked the
  true store in every synthetic catchment, by margins too small to survive real data. The
  recession slope reads the store only where recharge stops between events.
- **Do test the recharge rule.** It was identified in every synthetic catchment, by margins
  of 0.08 or more in log NSE, and whether baseflow rises with each event's quick flow points to
  split recharge before any calibration.
- **Before trusting a model in a severe drought, run the drought.** Pass a drought scenario
  through the spread of equally good fits. If the spread is wide, the record cannot answer
  the question, however good the calibration scores.

The study has limits. The catchments are synthetic, their structure is exactly the model's,
the gauge error is simple and the data are daily. On real data, structural error adds its own
equifinality, and the truth is not available to settle it. What carries over is the method:
know which parameters the record can see, and test a model where the record did not reach.

For a comparison with machine-learning models, the lesson is the same as for any model:
compare the flows, not the parameters, and compare them where the question lies. A score on
the record says little about a drought the record does not contain.

# Events across a sample

`find_events()` finds the events of a record objectively, by the method of Giani and others
(2022), and `event_scores()` scores a model on each ([Getting the floods
right](floods.html#finding-the-events) explains the method). `batch_events()` does both for
every basin of a batch. Here is a batch of eight synthetic catchments with two years of hourly
data each, calibrated automatically.

```{r ev-batch}
ev_basins <- file.path(tempdir(), "event-basins")
ev_output <- file.path(tempdir(), "event-projects")
unlink(c(ev_basins, ev_output), recursive = TRUE)
ev_sample <- synthetic_basins(ev_basins, n = 8, years = 2, dt = 1, seed = 21)
limited <- identical(toupper(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_")), "TRUE")
cores <- if (limited) 2L else min(4L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
# The made-up basins' rain is biased by a known factor, so the rainfall factor is searched.
ev_status <- calibrate_batch(ev_basins, ev_output, starts = 2, control = list(maxit = 30),
                          overrides = list(fc = c(0.6, 1.6)), cores = cores)
seconds <- system.time(found <- batch_events(ev_output))[["elapsed"]]
found$basins[, c("basin", "response_observed_h", "response_simulated_h", "events",
                 "median_abs_peak_error", "median_abs_timing_error_h")]
```

```{r ev-batch-numbers, include=FALSE}
b <- found$basins
e <- found$events
agree <- max(abs(b$response_observed_h - b$response_simulated_h))
```

Finding and scoring `r nrow(e)` events across `r nrow(b)` basins took `r f1(seconds)` seconds.
`r if (agree == 0) "In every basin the response time of the calibrated model matches the response time of the record" else paste0("In every basin the response time of the calibrated model is within ", agree, " hour", if (agree == 1) "" else "s", " of the response time of the record")`:
the models respond as fast as the catchments do.

Each event is labelled with the window that holds its observed peak, so performance on the
calibration and validation windows can be told apart. Events in the warm-up before
calibration (`outside`) are scored too, but a model is still settling there.

```{r by-period}
by_period <- aggregate(cbind(abs_peak_error = abs(peak_error),
                             abs_timing_error_h = abs(timing_error_h),
                             abs_volume_error = abs(volume_error)) ~ period, e,
                       stats::median)
by_period[-1] <- round(by_period[-1], 3)
by_period
```

The largest events matter most for flood forecasting, and they are the ones a whole-record
score is least able to describe. Here the largest tenth of each basin's events, by observed
peak, are set against the rest.

```{r by-size, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Peak error of each event, by observed peak relative to the basin's largest. Each point is one event; the line is a running median."}
e$relative_peak <- e$observed_peak / ave(e$observed_peak, e$basin, FUN = max)
e$largest <- ave(e$observed_peak, e$basin, FUN = function(x) x >= stats::quantile(x, 0.9))
plot(e$relative_peak, 100 * e$peak_error, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.4),
     log = "x", xlab = "Observed peak / basin's largest (log scale)",
     ylab = "Peak error (per cent)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = pal[7])
o <- order(e$relative_peak)
lines(e$relative_peak[o], 100 * stats::runmed(e$peak_error[o], 101), col = pal[3], lwd = 2)
size <- aggregate(cbind(peak_error = peak_error, timing_error_h = timing_error_h) ~ largest,
                  e, stats::median)
size
```

```{r size-numbers, include=FALSE}
ev_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * x)
big <- size$peak_error[size$largest == 1]
rest <- size$peak_error[size$largest == 0]
```

On the largest tenth of events the median peak is `r ev_pct(abs(big))` per cent
`r if (big < 0) "low" else "high"`, against `r ev_pct(abs(rest))` per cent
`r if (rest < 0) "low" else "high"` on the rest. A batch can then list the events that need a
look, the worst large ones first, without anyone searching the records by hand:

```{r worst}
worst <- e[e$largest == 1, ]
columns <- c("basin", "period", "flow_start_time", "observed_peak", "simulated_peak",
             "peak_error", "timing_error_h")
worst <- worst[order(-abs(worst$peak_error)), columns]
head(worst, 5)
```

```{r worst-numbers, include=FALSE}
top <- head(worst, 5)
gauged <- ev_sample$highest_gauged_m3s[match(top$basin, ev_sample$basin)]
above <- top$observed_peak > gauged
over_above <- sum(above & top$peak_error > 0)
```

Of these five, `r sum(above)` peaked above the basin's highest gauged flow, where the
synthetic rating records flow low`r if (over_above > 0) paste0(", and in ", over_above, " of them the model runs above the recorded peak") else ""`.
A large event that looks badly simulated may be a badly recorded one;
[Larger floods](extrapolation.html) explains how to tell.

## Speed

Estimating the response time is the costly part: the correlation is computed for every window
up to the longest response searched, by default 150 hours. The search runs in the compiled
core; `options(pdmS7.engine = "r")` runs the R reference instead. Here both are timed on ten
years of 15-minute data.

```{r speed}
quarter <- synthetic_catchment(synthetic_rain("2010-10-01", years = 10, dt = 0.25, seed = 4),
                               seed = 4)
rain <- quarter$forcing$rain
flow <- quarter$observed
compiled <- system.time(fast <- response_time_dmca(rain, flow, dt = 0.25))[["elapsed"]]
op <- options(pdmS7.engine = "r")
reference <- system.time(slow <- response_time_dmca(rain, flow, dt = 0.25))[["elapsed"]]
options(op)
all_events <- system.time(quarter_events <- find_events(rain, flow, dt = 0.25))[["elapsed"]]
c(steps = length(rain), windows = nrow(fast$curve), compiled_s = round(compiled, 2),
  r_s = round(reference, 1), same_answer = fast$response_h == slow$response_h,
  find_events_s = round(all_events, 2), events = nrow(quarter_events))
```

The compiled search took `r f2(compiled)` seconds against `r f1(reference)` in R, with the
same answer, and finding all `r nrow(quarter_events)` events took `r f2(all_events)` seconds
in all. A batch of hundreds of basins at 15 minutes is a matter of minutes.

## Limits

- **The time step must resolve the delay.** With daily data, a catchment that responds within
  a day shows a response time of one step, and its events are coarse. Hourly or finer data
  suit most British catchments.
- **The response time is not a time to peak or a lag of the whole hydrograph.** It is the
  timescale of the fast response; compare it like with like.
- **The method assumes rain drives flow.** Snowmelt, reservoirs and abstractions break that
  link, and events there need care.
- **Missing values count as zero** in the cumulative series, as in the published method, so
  long gaps in flow distort the response time. Fill or trim them first.
- **A smooth recession can run on to the next storm.** A flow window ends when the recession
  stops; on a very smooth record that may be the next event's rise.

`find_events()` is an independent implementation of the published method, from the paper and
the authors' reference code. Its tests check it on records with known storms and responses. It
was also checked against the authors' MATLAB code, run in Octave, on three synthetic records:
two years of hourly data from a fast and a slow catchment, and ten years of daily data. The
response times and all 663 event windows were identical. That check cannot run when this page
is built, so its result is stated here rather than computed.
